paper_title: Is Your Long-Horizon Benchmark Really Deep? Measuring and Synthesizing Depth in Terminal Tasks

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Long-horizon terminal tasks are used to evaluate and train agents. Human-curated datasets are scarce, so many synthesis methods have emerged. They usually measure the length of a task by the turns a model needs to pass it, and its difficulty by labels the LLM sets during generation. We find, however, that the turn count largely reflects the habits of the model, not only the demands of the task, and that the labels barely track how often models pass. We describe a terminal task by its work, the number of operations it requires, and its depth, the number of turns that must happen in sequence because the commands of each turn can only be chosen after reading the output of the previous one. Estimating depth as the smallest turn cap, stated to the agent, under which the task passes, we audit 734 tasks from six existing datasets. Synthesis has mostly added work, not depth: 94% of the solved synthetic tasks pass within three turns, yet depth, unlike the turn count, predicts difficulty beyond work. We propose DEPTH, in which a generation agent writes each task one segment at a time in a real software environment, carrying out each segment before writing it and starting the next from the state it leaves. Our 105 tasks exceed every audited dataset in depth and work, and none of six current models passes half of them. Fine-tuning Qwen3-8B on runs from these tasks improves it on two terminal benchmarks.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: An agent working in terminal issues shell commands in each turn, reads their output and decides what to run next, which lets it install software, configure services and debug programs (Merrill et al., 2026). Completing long tasks reliably, however, remains challenge (Kwa et al., 2025; Sinha et al., 2026): the agent must keep track of what it has learned about the environment over many turns, and an early mistake can derail every later step. Long-horizon terminal tasks are therefore needed both to evaluate agents and to train them. Each task bundles an instruction, an environment and an automatic verifier (Merrill et al., 2026; Harbor Framework Team, 2026), and training needs such tasks in large numbers (Pi et al., 2026; Raoof et al., 1 1 Introduction Preprint Figure 1. Work 𝑊 and depth 𝐷, as exchanges between the model and terminal; time runs downward. High 𝑊: many independent operations that fit in one turn. High 𝐷: chain of steps, each decided only after reading the output of the previous one. The commands are illustrative. 2026; Peng et al., 2026). Two kinds of methods provide them. Human-curated sets are written or reviewed by people: Terminal-Bench 2.0 (TB2; Merrill et al., 2026) consists of tasks written by people, and TerminalWorld-Verified (TW; Chu et al., 2026) builds tasks from real terminal recordings and has people review them. Synthesis methods generate tasks automatically (Cheng et al., 2026): TMax (Ivison et al., 2026) and SETA (Shen et al., 2026) generate tasks in bulk with controlled difficulty, CLI-Gym (Lin et al., 2026) derives repair tasks by breaking Dockerfiles, FACET (Shi et al., 2026b) composes skill packages into scenarios, and RST (Li et al., 2026b) extends verified tasks over recursive rounds, each perturbing the environment and rewriting the instruction and verifier. Both kinds have limitations. Human-curated sets are reliable but small and costly to extend, far from the numbers that training needs. Synthesis methods produce tasks in any number, but it is unclear whether these tasks are long in the sense that matters. They, like recent long-horizon benchmarks (Li et al., 2026a), report length as the number of turns or steps model takes under loose turn limit (Ivison et al., 2026; Shi et al., 2026b; Li et al., 2026b; Zou et al., 2026), count that reflects the habits of the model as much as the demands of the task (Meng et al., 2026; Desai et al., 2026). Difficulty is given by labels set during generation (Ivison et al., 2026; Shen et al., 2026), which record what was requested rather than what models find hard. Most of these pipelines verify only that each new task is solvable. Pipelines that aim for later steps to build on earlier ones obtain this by construction, such as chaining subtasks, adding hops or following dependency graphs (Xie et al., 2026; Shi et al., 2026a; Fan et al., 2026; Deng et al., 2026), or check it with an LLM that reads the task or trajectory (Zou et al., 2026; Wu et al., 2026). Neither measures whether later step requires the agent to read the output of an earlier one, so step can add operations without requiring the agent to look at the environment. When we state turn cap in the instruction and stop the agent once it is reached (turn-capped evaluation), most synthetic tasks pass within few turns; in many of them the agent issues every command in its first turn and never reads any output, so the task reduces to single-turn generation. Solving these problems matters for both uses: benchmark should test whether an agent can sustain long interaction, and training data should contain such interactions. What makes terminal task long? Many operations alone do not: task whose operations are independent can be completed by one script in one turn. task is long when the agent must, again and again, read the output of one command before it can decide the next. In the human-curated tasks that take many turns under cap, this need arises from details of real software that the agent 2 2 Preliminaries Preprint does not know in advance, such as the default configuration of specific version, the interface of an old release or truncated file in real format; in systems with several components, fixing one such problem often exposes the next. Configuration and version details are common cause of failures in deployed systems (Yin et al., 2011), and language models handle rarely documented and version-specific knowledge poorly (Kandpal et al., 2023; Misra et al., 2026). Task length thus has two separate dimensions, the amount of work and the number of turns that must happen in sequence, and the second largely comes from environments the agent cannot predict. Based on this observation, we describe terminal task by two quantities used in parallel computing, its work and its depth (Blelloch, 1996). As illustrated in Figure 1, the work 𝑊 is the number of operations needed to complete the task when the state of the environment is known; the depth 𝐷 is the number of turns that must happen in sequence, because the commands of each turn can only be chosen after reading the output of the previous one. We estimate 𝑊 by the number of lines 𝑊 of the reference solution, and 𝐷 by turn-capped evaluation: the smallest cap under which the task passes is recorded as 𝐷. With these estimates we audit six existing datasets and find that existing synthesis methods primarily increase work rather than depth. We also find that tasks with both high work and high depth are substantially more challenging for current models. To obtain tasks that are large in both, we propose Depth, in which generation agent Derives Each segment of task by Performing and Testing it in real software environment, Handing the state it leaves to the next segment. Each task consists of segments delivered one at time in the same session, so later segments depend on what earlier ones changed. The resulting tasks exhibit greater work and depth than any of the six audited datasets, while providing meaningful discrimination across models with different capabilities. As shown in Table 2, even frontier models achieve pass rates below 50%, highlighting the difficulty of these tasks. Beyond evaluation, trajectories collected from these tasks also serve as training data: fine-tuning small open model on them improves its performance on existing single-instruction terminal benchmarks (Merrill et al., 2026; The Terminal-Bench Team, 2026; OpenThoughts Agent team et al., 2026). Our contributions are as follows. 1. Measurement and audit. We describe terminal-task length by work 𝑊 and depth 𝐷, estimate 𝐷 per task by turn-capped evaluation, and use it to audit six existing datasets, finding that synthesis methods mainly add work. 2. Construction and evaluation. We build deep terminal tasks from real software environments by segmented generation, and show that they are substantially deeper than existing datasets and challenging for current models. 3. Training. We show that fine-tuning Qwen3-8B (Yang et al., 2025a) on trajectories from our tasks improves its performance on two existing terminal benchmarks. We discuss related work in Appendix A.

sections.title: 3.2 Seed Environments
sections.content: We draw seed environments from public terminal-task packages, mostly the 1,530 packages of TerminalWorld (Chu et al., 2026); each package comes with software environment built from Dockerfile. After filtering by rules, an LLM judge rates each environment on whether its components are real software rather than stand-ins, whether several of them work together, whether the software is uncommon, and whether it can support several segments of work. Keeping at most one environment for each kind of system, we collected 136 seed environments. Generation and evaluation both run without network access, so the generation agent meets the problems the evaluated agent will meet, and reference solutions can be replayed later.

sections.title: 3.5 Training Data
sections.content: We turn runs on our tasks into data for supervised fine-tuning (SFT). We collect runs without turn cap from the six models we evaluate, and from each run we keep the segments that pass in row from the first one. These runs often exceed the context window of the model being trained, and at evaluation terminus-2 then compresses the context into summary of the work so far and questions and answers about it. We therefore cut each run where terminus-2 would compress it and start the next sample from this summary and these questions and answers, so that the trained model also learns to continue after compression. We fine-tune Qwen3-8B on the resulting samples.

sections.title: 4.3 Depth Predicts Difficulty
sections.content: Public pass rates. TB2 and TW release per-task results of other models: the mean pass rate over 15 leaderboard submissions for TB2, and the share of eight models that solve each task for TW. We call these public pass rates. We relate them to 𝐷 by rank partial correlation (Conover & Iman, 1981), which replaces each variable by its rank and correlates two of them after removing the linear effect of third, such as 𝑊. Depth predicts difficulty beyond work. The left panel of Figure 4 shows that, once 𝑊 is controlled, tasks with larger 𝐷 have lower public pass rates: the rank partial correlation is 0.31 on the 105 solved TB2 and TW tasks and 0.49 on TB2 alone. On our tasks, the same test uses the mean pass rate of GLM-5.3-Flash, GPT-6 Luna, MiMo-V2.6-Flash and GPT-6.1 Sol; because GLM-5.3-Flash is one of them, 𝐷 here comes from DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash alone. Over the 52 solved tasks with results from all four, the correlation is 0.29 (95% CI 0.53 to 0.02), close to that of the human-curated sets, and 0.31 when the two are pooled. Turn counts do not predict difficulty once depth is known. Controlling for 𝐷, 𝑁 is unrelated to the public pass rate on TB2 and TW (+0.06, 95% CI 0.18 to +0.26; open circle in Figure 4). Difficulty labels from generation barely track pass rates. As Figure 8 shows, the labels set during generation correlate with the released pass rates at only 0.07 to 0.11, and those in the task files of TW not at all, while the ratings of TB2 authors reach 0.46. Depth agrees with the ratings of task authors. Of the six datasets, only TB2 states that its difficulty labels are written by people: each task author rates the task as easy, medium or hard. Nine of the 11 sampled tasks rated hard have 𝐷 2, against 8 of the 28 rated easy or medium (right panel of Figure 4). On the 37 solved tasks, the rank partial correlation of the rating with 𝐷 controlling for 𝑊 is +0.55 (95% CI +0.29 to +0.75), while those of 𝑊 and 𝑁 with the rating, each controlling for 𝐷, are not significant (+0.16 and 0.28, both CIs containing zero). 4 Experiments Preprint Figure 5. Splitting the TB2 and TW tasks at 𝐷 = 2 and at the median 𝑊, the tasks large in both have mean within-dataset percentile of the public pass rate of 0.29 (lower is harder), against 0.53 to 0.59 for the other three groups; task large in only one of the two is not harder.

sections.title: 4.4 Our Tasks
sections.content: Our tasks are deep and large. Each of the 105 tasks comes from different seed environment and has three to six segments, six for most. DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash solves 54 of them, and 44 of these have 𝐷 40 (Figure 3). Their median 𝑊 is 315 lines, above the 90th percentile of 𝑊 over solved tasks of the existing synthetic datasets (226 lines), and their median 𝑁 is 45 turns, against 5 to 9 for the existing datasets  (Table 1)  . Depth does not come from delivering segments. Each segment takes at least one turn, so 𝐷 is at least the number of segments, at most six, while 44 tasks have 𝐷 40. To remove this bound, we merge the segments of 25 randomly sampled tasks into one instruction and measure 𝐷 again. As shown in Figure 5, 𝐷 does not decrease for 68% of them. Of the tasks whose 𝐷 drops, most drop by only one cap, suggesting that depth comes mainly from what the tasks require. Depth does not come from the seed environments. Of the 54 seed environments of our solved tasks, 35 are released with an original task whose 𝐷 can be measured. Paired with our tasks from the same environments, these original tasks have 𝐷 10 in 34 pairs and 𝐷 = 1 in 26, while ours have 𝐷 20 and the higher 𝐷 in all 35 (sign test, 𝑝 = 5.8 1011). Checks see key steps and the dependence between segments. When we replay reference solutions with parts removed, the checks of segment fail before the segment is done in 601 of 602 segments (99.8%) and fail when its key step is removed in 598 of 604 (99.0%). With the key step removed, the next segment also fails in 421 of 500 cases (84.2%), so later segments build on what the key step produces. We show more details in Appendix F. Cost. Generation cost $113.66 for the 136 seed environments, from which 105 tasks were accepted (77%): about $1.08 per accepted task, excluding evaluation and the measurement of 𝐷.

sections.title: 4.6 Fine-Tuning
sections.content: Setup. We fine-tune Qwen3-8B (Yang et al., 2025a) on 4,941 samples built from 1,272 runs on our tasks and evaluate it in terminus-2 on Terminal-Bench 2.1 (TB2.1; The Terminal-Bench Team, 2026) and OpenThoughts-TBLite (TBLite; OpenThoughts Agent team et al., 2026), with three runs per task. None of the tasks used for training is built from either benchmark. Both benchmarks give all requirements in one instruction. The baseline is the base model in the same non-thinking mode with the same sampling parameters. Fine-tuning improves performance on both TB2.1 and TBLite. As Figure 7 shows, pass@1 rises from 2.6% to 4.9% on TB2.1 and from 3.4% to 9.1% on TBLite, and the fine-tuned model also exceeds the thinking mode of the base model on both. Runs on tasks delivered in segments thus carry over to tasks given in one instruction.

sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: We presented Depth, which measures the depth of terminal task, the number of turns that must happen in sequence, by turn-capped evaluation, and builds tasks that are large in both work and depth. The measurement shows that existing synthesis methods have mostly added work rather than depth, 11 References Preprint Figure 7. Qwen3-8B before and after fine-tuning on runs from our tasks. We fine-tune and evaluate in the non-thinking mode; the thinking mode of the base model is shown for reference. Bars are the mean pass@1 over three runs, and error bars one standard deviation. and that once work is controlled, deeper tasks are harder for other models. By having generation agent carry out each segment in real software environment and start the next segment from the state it leaves, Depth builds 105 tasks that are deeper and larger than those of every audited dataset; frontier models pass fewer than half of them, and fine-tuning small open model on runs from these tasks improves it on two existing terminal benchmarks. These results suggest that the length of task should be measured rather than assumed, and we recommend that builders of benchmarks and training data report depth alongside work.

sections.title: A Related Work
sections.content: Benchmarks for long-horizon agents. Agents that act in computer environments are evaluated on resolving repository issues (Jimenez et al., 2024), on terminal tasks (Merrill et al., 2026; Chu et al., 2026) and on security vulnerabilities, where SecProbe (Luo et al., 2026) synthesizes repository-scale repair tasks on demand and chooses them adaptively with item response theory. Benchmarks that target long horizons report the length of task as the time human expert needs (Kwa et al., 2025) or as the turns or steps model takes (Li et al., 2026a; Desai et al., 2026), or make tasks long by chaining milestones on one codebase (Deng et al., 2026). Related studies examine how reliability declines as tasks get longer (Sinha et al., 2026). These measures describe what model does under loose limit. We instead state turn cap and record the smallest cap under which task passes, which estimates the turns that must happen in sequence rather than the turns model happens to take. Synthesizing tasks for agents. Training agents requires verifiable tasks and trajectories in large numbers (Pi et al., 2026; Raoof et al., 2026; Zou et al., 2026), and many pipelines synthesize them. Software-engineering tasks are built by injecting bugs into real repositories (Yang et al., 2025b), and tool-use and computer-use tasks are generated automatically (Shi et al., 2026a; Xie et al., 2026). For the terminal, pipelines derive tasks from agent skills, skill graphs and agent trajectories (Cheng et al., 2026; Fan et al., 2026; Wu et al., 2026), break environments (Lin et al., 2026), and scale environments for reinforcement learning (Peng et al., 2026); the synthetic datasets we audit, TMax (Ivison et al., 2026), SETA (Shen et al., 2026), FACET (Shi et al., 2026b) and RST (Li et al., 2026b), belong to this line. Synthetic trajectories also train components other than the agent, as in AuraGen (Huang et al., 2026), which injects risks of calibrated difficulty into agent trajectories to train guardrail that checks plans before they are executed. Pipelines that aim for later steps to build on earlier ones obtain this by construction or check it with an LLM (Xie et al., 2026; Shi et al., 2026a; Wu et al., 2026). We instead let generation agent carry out each segment in the container before writing the next, and measure the depth of the resulting tasks. Synthetic data generated by LLMs. Beyond agent tasks, LLMs generate training and evaluation data across domains, and recent pipelines control what is generated and verify it before use. DataGen (Huang et al., 2025b) is unified framework for generating text datasets that uses attribute-guided generation for diversity, code-based checks for label correctness and retrieval for factual accuracy. ChemOrch (Huang et al., 2025a) synthesizes chemistry instructions with controlled diversity and difficulty and builds the responses with tools, repairing them from tool feedback. SpecAlign (Wang et al., 2026) turns model specifications written by providers into preference data through rule annotation and adversarial multi-agent synthesis. Ma et al. (2026b) simulate multi-turn interactions among user, assistant and distractor agents to synthesize data for personalization, and SkillGen (Ma et al., 2026a) induces reusable skills from successful and failed agent trajectories and verifies each skill by comparing outcomes on the same instances with and without it. Our pipeline likewise verifies what it generates, but by execution in the environment itself: the reference solution is replayed in fresh container, and the checks of each segment are written to fail when its key step is removed.

sections.content: Order of runs. DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash first runs every task twice without cap. If neither run passes, it gives no estimate for the task. Otherwise, let 𝑁𝑚 be the fewest turns among its passing runs; the 𝑁 reported in the main text is that of DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash. Caps at or above 𝑁𝑚 count as passed without being run, since run has already passed within 𝑁𝑚 turns. The caps below 𝑁𝑚 are tried in increasing order with up to two runs each, the second run being skipped once the first passes, and the first cap with passing run gives 𝐷𝑚. If no cap below 𝑁𝑚 passes, 𝐷𝑚 is the smallest cap at or above 𝑁𝑚, or above the largest cap if 𝑁𝑚 exceeds it. 15 Measurement Details Preprint Second model. GLM-5.3-Flash runs only at the caps below the estimate of DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, with up to two runs per cap and no runs without cap. It can therefore only lower 𝐷, and it is not run on tasks with 𝐷 = 1 or on tasks that DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash does not solve. Stating the cap. Under cap 𝑇, the following text is appended to the instruction of an existing task:

sections.title: Turn limit appended to the instruction
sections.content: Turn limit: you have at most 𝑇 turns for this task. One turn is one of your responses; response may contain several commands. The session is cut off after turn 𝑇 and whatever state the environment is in will be graded. Plan for this limit: batch commands where you can, and do not spend turns on steps that are not needed. In multi-segment tasks the cap covers all segments together, the text says so (for the whole task, all 𝑘 parts together) and adds that parts not finished by turn 𝑇 fail, and every new segment reports the turns used so far. The harness stops the run after turn 𝑇. Harness. Existing tasks and ours run in the same harness, terminus-2, and Table 3 compares its settings with those in the papers of the audited datasets, four of which also use terminus-2. After each turn, the agent sees the output produced since the previous turn, cut to 10,000 bytes by keeping the first and last 5,000. Commands do not block: for each command, the agent states how long to wait before the output is read, at most 60 seconds, and command still running after that is waited for in later turn. Both are defaults of terminus-2 and apply to all tasks alike. Without cap, run may take up to 150 turns. An existing task has 30 minutes, which replaces the agent time limit set by its dataset; this is longer than that limit for 477 of the 631 sampled tasks that set one, equal for 88 and shorter for 66, mostly SETA tasks with 60 minutes. Our tasks have 3 hours, or 2.5 and 1.5 hours for the 4 tasks with five segments and the 3 with three. All other parts of existing tasks are used as released. Delivering segments. We extend terminus-2 to run the segments of task in one conversation and one container; everything else, including its prompt templates and context compression, is unchanged. The first message announces the number of parts and explains the protocol: Start of the first message of multi-segment task This task is handed to you in 𝑘 parts, one at time, in this same terminal session. Below is part 1. When part is done, set "task_complete": true; the next part is then sent to you. Later parts build on what earlier parts left in the environment. Each part is graded when you mark it complete, and you are not told the grade; the task passes only if every part does. When the agent marks segment complete, its checks run, and the harness sends Part 𝑖 1 is marked complete. Here is part 𝑖 of 𝑘 with the next instruction and the current terminal screen as new message. Later instructions are never placed in the container, and the checks of segment are removed from the container before the next segment starts, so the agent can read neither in advance. run stops at the first segment that fails. terminus-2 asks the agent once to confirm that it is done; we keep this confirmation only in the last segment, since in earlier segments it would add one turn per segment and inflate 𝐷. Choice of models. model used to measure depth must merge commands into fewer turns once told the cap; otherwise it measures work. We test this on calibration tasks in which every step is solved by one short command. In the parallel tasks, ten independent steps are listed in one file. In the static-chain tasks, each of ten steps needs the answer to the previous one, but every step is written in plain file from the start. Both can be completed in two or three turns by writing script. sections.title: C Dataset Selection and Sampling
sections.content: Datasets. We audit datasets of terminal tasks that release runnable task packages, each with an instruction, Docker environment and verifier. We evaluate four synthetic datasets: TMax, FACET, RST, and SETA. Among human-curated sets, TB2 consists of tasks written and verified by people, and TW is the subset of TerminalWorld that people reviewed, built from real terminal recordings. Sampling rules. The same rules apply to every dataset. 17 Dataset Selection and Sampling Preprint 1. Only tasks that at least one model passes in the released results are drawn, since task that no model passes gives no estimate of 𝐷; in the hardest level of TMax, only 1 of the 59 tasks with released Gemini runs was ever passed. FACET and part of SETA release no per-task results and are drawn at random. 2. Tasks are split into groups by the length or difficulty the dataset reports  (Table 4)  , drawn within each group with fixed seed, and interleaved across groups, so that every prefix of the list is balanced across groups. 3. Only tasks with light dependencies are kept: they run in an ordinary Docker container without GPUs, privileged mode or systemd, use no external services, and need neither downloads above 200 MB nor builds above 1 GB or 10 minutes. We decide by reading the instruction, Dockerfile, reference solution and verifier of each task, and build the image once when unsure. 4. Once the image is built, the reference solution must get full marks and doing nothing must get zero; tasks that fail this check are replaced by the next ones in the list. 5. Tasks are used as released, without changing their instructions, environments or verifiers. TB2 and TW are small, so all their tasks that meet the rules and pass the check are included. FACET and RST have low shares of solved tasks, so their lists are extended under the same rules until about 50 tasks are solved, which is why they have the most sampled tasks. Table 4. sections.content: A Preprint check script is bash file in which every check prints one line, PASS name or FAIL name: reason; the segment passes if every check passes, and script that stops before its last line fails. The generation agent writes checks with the functions in Table 7, which also do the comparing, so the agent decides only what to ask the system and what the answer must be. Table 7. Letter case, runs of spaces, and spaces around : and = are ignored in patterns and outputs; key and column names ignore case and treat -, _ and spaces alike; values lose surrounding spaces and quotes. The kinds int, num and version compare the first number or dotted version in each value, so 5.7.21-log equals 5.7.21 as version. bool maps yes, true, pass, ok, on and 1 to true and their opposites to false. set compares the items of two lists regardless of order and repeats, and seq compares them in order, for requirements such as before Y. An empty expected value fails, except that two empty sets are equal. Readers accept missing header line, tabs, commas, tables and aligned columns. Every command runs under 120-second limit, and check script must finish within 10 minutes. Rules for writing checks. Besides the three rules in the main text, the generation agent follows these: Expected values are computed from the live system when the checks run; counts, identifiers, versions or states seen during generation are never written into check. Report files are read only through the readers, by the field and column names the agent declares; the pipeline writes the exact format into the instruction. 23 Our Dataset Preprint An event the goal asks for, such as restart or failover, is checked through trace the software itself keeps, such as later start time than component that was not restarted or line in its own log. file the agent writes about the event is not evidence, and an event that leaves no trace cannot be deliverable. string looked for in the files of the solver must appear in the instruction or be printed by the software itself, not by script the agent wrote. running service is checked by talking to it with its own client; processes are checked only when the instruction asks for process. When the message of tool and the real state disagree, or two readings of requirement are defensible, both are accepted. Values that must be measured never appear among the names stated in the instruction, so checks cannot depend on them. Replays with parts removed. sections.title: H Merging Segments into One Instruction
sections.content: We draw 25 tasks at random from the solved tasks whose 𝐷 had been measured when we ran this experiment and turn each into task with single segment. The environment and the work stay the same: the instruction gives the requirements of all segments at once in their original order, the reference solution runs the scripts of all segments in order, and the checks of all segments run together on the final state. Checks of earlier segments that later segment is meant to change, such as port that the last segment moves, are found by running the merged reference solution and dropped. merged task 26 Evaluation Details Preprint passes the quality check if the reference solution then passes all remaining checks, including every check of the last segment. We measure the merged tasks with DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash alone and without runs without cap. Only caps up to the original 𝐷 of DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash are tried, from the largest downward, with two runs per cap, stopping at the first cap where both runs fail. The 𝐷 of merged task is the smallest cap passed, and merged task that fails at the original 𝐷 is counted as not solved within it. For 17 of the 25 tasks, 𝐷 does not decrease: 8 pass at the original cap and 9 are not solved within it. Of the remaining 8, 7 drop by one cap level and 1 by two.

sections.title: I Evaluation Details
sections.content: Setup. All models run in the multi-segment version of terminus-2 with the limits used to measure 𝐷: 150 turns and the time limit of the task. The open-weight models and GPT-6 Luna are called through OpenRouter with the serving provider fixed: DeepSeek, Together or Wafer for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, Fireworks for GLM-5.3-Flash, Xiaomi for MiMo-V2.6-Flash and OpenAI for GPT-6 Luna. GPT-6.1 Sol and Claude Sonnet 5.5 are called through TokenRouter. We set the reasoning effort only for GPT-6 Luna (medium) and keep the default of the provider for the other models, which gives the levels in Table 2. The runs of DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash for evaluation are separate from those for measuring 𝐷: it passes 52 tasks in its two evaluation runs, all among the 54 it solves when 𝐷 is measured. Refusals. The provider of GPT-6.1 Sol refused requests on 7 tasks as possible cybersecurity risk, and retries were refused as well. On 12 tasks, the safety classifier of Anthropic refused requests from Claude Sonnet 5.5 (Anthropic, 2026b), returning refusal without content and ending the run. On 3 more tasks Claude Sonnet 5.5 returned empty responses and gave no valid result. The 7 tasks refused for GPT-6.1 Sol are all among these 15. The refused tasks mostly concern system security, although every task runs offline. task without valid result is left out of the denominator of that model; the other four models have valid runs on all 105 tasks. Failure modes. Figure 14 classifies every run without cap by how it ends. GPT-6 Luna and GLM-5.3Flash often submit within three turns without verifying their work (18% and 20%), failure that the taxonomy of agent failures in Terminal-Bench also lists (Merrill et al., 2026). GLM-5.3-Flash also breaks the terminal session in 13% of its runs. MiMo-V2.6-Flash rarely submits early but spends long on each turn and reaches the time limit of segment or the turn limit in 33% of its runs. Figure 14. Outcome of every run without cap on our tasks, as share of each models runs. Failed runs are classed by how they stop. The three cases below show how runs end early or run out of time. Training Data Details Preprint Submitting without checking (Pacemaker, segment 1, GPT-6 Luna) Pacemaker manages resources in Linux high-availability clusters. The instruction asks for five fault-injection operations in given order, with their output saved to log. GPT-6 Luna sent all five commands in one turn. The first lacked the flag for automatic confirmation and stopped to wait for input, which swallowed the commands after it, so the log recorded the operations in the wrong order. GPT-6 Luna ended the segment without reading the output. Breaking the terminal (Laravel application, segment 3, GLM-5.3-Flash) GLM-5.3-Flash had complete plan but began batch of commands with set -e, which makes the shell exit as soon as command fails. In an interactive shell the setting persists: later command returned nonzero status, the shell exited, and the session ended together with the remaining segments. Most broken sessions of GLM-5.3-Flash and GPT-6 Luna come from set -e or exit. Reaching the time limit (Spark with Spooq, segment 1, MiMo-V2.6-Flash) The instruction asks to run sample job in the Spark shell and save its output. Two problems stand in the way: the wrong entry point causes null-pointer exception, and the job lowers the log level to WARN, which hides the line the output needs. MiMo-V2.6-Flash found the first cause, then kept reading bytecode to trace the second without first saving an output that would pass, and ran out of time.

sections.title: J Training Data Details
sections.content: At evaluation, terminus-2 compresses the context through three calls: the model summarizes the work so far, asks questions in new context that holds the instruction, the summary and the current screen, and answers them from the old context. The runs we collect come from long-context models and contain no compression, so model trained on them would never see what follows one; we therefore cut each run where terminus-2 would compress it. The sample after cut starts with the messages terminus-2 would give the model, with the summary, questions and answers generated by an LLM and the instruction covering all segments delivered so far. The three calls also become samples with prose targets. Replies the harness cannot parse are kept with its error message but excluded from the loss.
